title: Anatomy and Physiology: Respiratory, Digestive and Immune Systems
summary: Three systems that all handle the outside world — air, food and everything living that arrives with them. Work from the structure to the function it permits, and from the function to the disease that appears when the structure fails.
objectives: Trace air from the nose to the alveolus and name the structure doing each job along the way.
Read a spirogram for lung volumes and capacities and classify the pattern as obstructive or restrictive.
Explain gas exchange and oxygen transport, and predict which way a dissociation curve shifts.
Follow a meal along the alimentary canal, naming the wall layer, lining, enzyme and accessory organ acting at each point.
Distinguish innate from adaptive immunity and name the cell, receptor and molecule doing the work in each.
Match a respiratory, digestive or immune disorder to the structure or process it damages.

units.title: The Breathing Apparatus
units.summary: The lung is a branching tube that ends in a membrane thin enough for gas to cross, hung inside a sealed cavity. Every respiratory question depends on one of those three facts.
objectives: Distinguish the conducting zone from the respiratory zone and name the structures of each.
Explain how the pleura and the diaphragm let a muscle in the abdomen move air in the chest.

lessons.title: The Airway from Nose to Bronchiole
lessons.objective: Order the structures of the conducting zone from nasal cavity to terminal bronchiole and state what each contributes to warming, filtering and delivering air.

lessons.title: Alveoli and the Surface Gas Must Cross
lessons.objective: Describe the alveolus, its cell types and its surfactant, and explain why the barrier between air and blood must stay thin and moist.

lessons.title: Pleura, Diaphragm and the Sealed Chest
lessons.objective: Name the pleural layers and their fluid, explain how intrapleural pressure couples lung to chest wall, and describe what the diaphragm and intercostal muscles do on inspiration.

units.title: Ventilation and Its Measurement
units.summary: Breathing is a pressure argument, and the spirometer is how that argument gets scored. Volumes and capacities are the vocabulary every clinical respiratory question is written in.
objectives: Explain inspiration and expiration as pressure changes and name the common patterns of breathing.
Define each lung volume and capacity and locate it on a spirogram.

lessons.title: How a Breath Actually Happens
lessons.objective: Explain inhalation and exhalation as volume and pressure changes, and distinguish quiet breathing, hyperventilation, hypoventilation and apnea.

lessons.title: Volumes, Capacities and What They Add Up To
lessons.objective: Define tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual volumes, and build vital capacity, inspiratory capacity, functional residual capacity and total lung capacity from them.

lessons.title: Reading a Spirogram
lessons.objective: Compute FEV1 and FVC from a spirogram, use their ratio to separate an obstructive from a restrictive pattern, and say what a bronchodilator response adds.

units.title: Gas Transport and Its Control
units.summary: Air in the alveolus is useless until oxygen is on a hemoglobin molecule and carbon dioxide is on its way out. The curve and the chemoreceptor are where those two exchanges are examined.
objectives: Predict the direction of gas movement from partial pressures on either side of a membrane.
Explain how oxygen binding, carbon dioxide carriage and blood pH set the pace of breathing.

lessons.title: Partial Pressures and Diffusion
lessons.objective: Use partial pressure differences to predict the direction and rate of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement between alveolus, blood and tissue.

lessons.title: Hemoglobin and the Dissociation Curve
lessons.objective: Explain cooperative oxygen binding, read percent saturation off a dissociation curve, and predict the shift produced by pH, carbon dioxide, temperature and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

lessons.title: Respiratory Rhythm, Chemoreceptors and Blood Gases
lessons.objective: Name the brainstem centres that generate respiratory rhythm, explain which chemoreceptor responds to which stimulus, and classify a blood gas result as respiratory acidosis or alkalosis.

units.title: Lungs Under Load and Under Disease
units.summary: Exercise and altitude push a healthy lung to its limit; disease moves the limit inward. The same measurements describe both.
objectives: Describe the respiratory response to exercise and the acclimatisation response to altitude.
Match each named lung disease to the structure it damages and the test that detects it.

lessons.title: Exercise and High Altitude
lessons.objective: Describe how ventilation, oxygen consumption and cardiac output change during exercise, and explain acclimatisation and the altitude illnesses that follow when it fails.

lessons.title: COPD, Asthma, Cystic Fibrosis and Sleep Apnea
lessons.objective: Distinguish chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, cystic fibrosis and sleep apnea by the airway or alveolar change each produces and how each is diagnosed.

lessons.title: Pneumonia, Tuberculosis, Fibrosis and Lung Cancer
lessons.objective: Identify pneumonia, tuberculosis, pleurisy, pulmonary edema, pulmonary fibrosis, the pneumoconioses and lung cancer from the compartment of the lung each involves.

lessons.title: Drugs, Oxygen, Surgery and Prevention
lessons.objective: Match bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, oxygen therapy, CPAP, mechanical ventilation, transplantation and smoking cessation to the respiratory problem each addresses.

units.title: The Gut as a Tube
units.summary: The alimentary canal is one continuous tube with the same four layers from esophagus to anus; only the lining changes, and it changes for a reason.
objectives: Name the organs of the alimentary canal and the accessory organs that empty into it.
Identify the four layers of the gut wall and the lining characteristic of each region.

lessons.title: The Canal and the Organs That Feed It
lessons.objective: Order the organs of the alimentary canal from mouth to anus and state what each accessory organ secretes into the tube.

lessons.title: Mucosa, Submucosa, Muscularis, Serosa
lessons.objective: Identify the four layers of the gut wall in order from the lumen outward and name the nerve plexus and sublayer found in each.

lessons.title: Why Each Region Has the Lining It Has
lessons.objective: Contrast the epithelium of the esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine and relate each to the abrasion, acid or absorption that region handles.

units.title: Breaking Food Down
units.summary: Mechanical digestion makes the pieces smaller and chemical digestion makes them absorbable; the liver and pancreas supply most of what does the chemistry.
objectives: Distinguish mechanical from chemical digestion and name the motility pattern behind each.
Pair each digestive enzyme with its substrate, its source and its product.

lessons.title: Chewing, Churning and Peristalsis
lessons.objective: Distinguish mechanical from chemical digestion and explain how mastication, peristalsis, segmentation and the sphincters move a bolus into chyme and onward.

lessons.title: Enzymes, Substrates and Absorption
lessons.objective: Name the enzyme, its source and its products for protein, fat and carbohydrate digestion, and explain how bile makes fat digestible.

lessons.title: The Liver, the Pancreas and Kupffer Cells
lessons.objective: State the liver's and pancreas's digestive roles and describe what Kupffer cells do to material arriving from the gut.

units.title: When Digestion Goes Wrong
units.summary: Most named digestive diseases are a failure of one of three things: the acid barrier, the absorptive surface, or the liver. Sorting a case into one of those three is most of the work.
objectives: Trace an acid-related, an inflammatory and a malabsorptive disease to the tissue each damages.
Relate obesity and chronic liver injury to digestive cancer risk.

lessons.title: Reflux, Gastritis and Peptic Ulcers
lessons.objective: Explain how reflux, Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs injure the mucosa, and distinguish GERD, gastritis and peptic ulcer disease by site and cause.

lessons.title: IBD, Celiac Disease and the Malabsorbing Gut
lessons.objective: Distinguish Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, celiac disease, diverticular disease, lactose intolerance and appendicitis by the region and layer of bowel each affects.

lessons.title: Hepatitis, Obesity and Digestive Cancers
lessons.objective: Contrast hepatitis A, B and C by transmission and outcome, and relate chronic liver injury and obesity to cirrhosis and to esophageal, stomach, colorectal and liver cancer.

units.title: Immune Anatomy and the First Response
units.summary: Immunity has addresses as well as cells: marrow makes them, the thymus trains them, and nodes and spleen are where they meet an antigen. Everything before that meeting is innate.
objectives: Locate the primary and secondary lymphoid organs and say what happens in each.
Describe barriers, complement and pattern recognition as defences that act without prior exposure.

lessons.title: Marrow, Thymus, Spleen, Nodes and Skin
lessons.objective: Distinguish primary from secondary lymphoid organs and state the immune function of bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes and skin.

lessons.title: Barriers, Complement and Pattern Recognition
lessons.objective: Explain how physical and chemical barriers, the complement pathways and Toll-like receptors detect and attack a pathogen before any antibody exists.

lessons.title: Inflammation and the Cells That Arrive First
lessons.objective: Order the events of an inflammatory response and state what neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells and dendritic cells each contribute.

units.title: Adaptive Immunity
units.summary: The adaptive system is slower because it is specific, and specific because a cell had to be selected and expanded first. Memory is the payoff.
objectives: Explain antigen presentation and the division of labour between T and B cells.
Contrast a primary with a secondary response and place the allergic response among them.

lessons.title: T Cells, B Cells and MHC
lessons.objective: Explain how an antigen-presenting cell displays antigen on MHC, and contrast what helper and cytotoxic T cells and B cells do once they recognise it.

lessons.title: Antibodies, Memory and Allergy
lessons.objective: Name the immunoglobulin classes and their jobs, contrast primary and secondary responses, and describe how an IgE-mediated allergic reaction unfolds.

units.title: When Immunity Misfires
units.summary: The same machinery causes disease three ways: by over-reacting, by under-performing, and by aiming at the body itself.
objectives: Classify a reaction into one of the four hypersensitivity types from its mechanism and timing.
Distinguish immunodeficiency from autoimmunity and name the defect in each named disorder.

lessons.title: The Four Hypersensitivities
lessons.objective: Assign anaphylaxis, urticaria, myasthenia gravis, serum sickness and the Arthus reaction to hypersensitivity types I through IV and justify each by mechanism.

lessons.title: Immunodeficiency: HIV, CVID and SCID
lessons.objective: Explain which immune compartment fails in HIV infection, common variable immunodeficiency and severe combined immunodeficiency, and what infections follow from each.

lessons.title: Autoimmunity: Nerve, Thyroid, Joint and Skin
lessons.objective: Name the self-target in multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves' disease, lupus, scleroderma, dermatomyositis and psoriasis and its arthritis.

units.title: Transplants and Immune Therapy
units.summary: Two places where immunology is deliberately steered: a graft that must not be rejected, and a tumour that must be.
objectives: Classify grafts and explain why matching and immunosuppression prevent rejection.
Describe how antibody, checkpoint and cell therapies redirect immunity against cancer.

lessons.title: Grafts, Matching and Rejection
lessons.objective: Distinguish autograft, allograft, isograft and xenograft, and explain how tissue matching and immunosuppressive drugs reduce hyperacute, acute and chronic rejection.

lessons.title: Immunotherapy, CAR-T and Everyday Immune Drugs
lessons.objective: Explain how monoclonal antibodies, immune checkpoint inhibitors and CAR T-cell therapy act, and match corticosteroids, antihistamines and vaccines to the immune problem each treats.
